national.body: Hunger is expected to worsen in 16 countries over the next six months, with war-torn Sudan and Yemen among five nations facing the gravest risk, the United Nations' food agencies warned Friday. The agencies pointed to conflict, soaring fuel costs linked to war in the Middle East and steep cuts in aid. The Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Food Program's Hunger Hotspots report covers December through May 2026. It places Sudan, Yemen, South Sudan, Somalia and northern Nigeria at the highest level of concern. In Yemen, the report said, hunger is likely to worsen as fighting that resumed in July spreads across multiple fronts. All five have appeared on the list repeatedly since 2022. The Palestinian territories were moved down one level following the October 2025 ceasefire in Gaza, though 67% of Gaza's population still faces crisis-level hunger or worse, and the report warned that the gains were fragile. Yemen has been at war since 2014, when the Iran-backed Houthi rebels seized the capital, Sanaa, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene the following year. The Houthis' encirclement of the southwestern city of Taiz has created siege-like conditions there, and more than 300,000 people have been displaced since the escalation began in July, mostly in Taiz, Lahj and Aden provinces. In government-held areas, 1.8 million people face emergency levels of hunger, up from 1.6 million in the previous analysis. No recent assessment exists for areas held by the Houthis, which have become harder for aid groups to reach as the conflict has intensified. The last nationwide projection, which ran through February, found 18.3 million people, more than half the population, in crisis or worse. Yemen relies heavily on imported food and fuel, and the report warned that attacks on Red Sea shipping threaten that lifeline. Shipping is now disrupted in the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea and the Black Sea. Gulf fertilizer shipments remain largely halted.

national.summary: The alleged incident follows a series of breaches and outages that have been reported at federal agencies this month.
national.body: The U.S. Air Force's cloud computing platform was breached in a cyberattack, multiple sources told Reuters on Friday.The hackers breached Cloud One, the Air Force's flagship cloud computing platform, according to Reuters, potentially exposing sensitive military and personnel information.The breach was discovered at some point in the last month during system upgrades, sources told the outlet. In a statement provided to CBS News, an Air Force spokesperson did not confirm or deny the breach, saying that it "does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities, or operational status of specific networks and systems.""Ensuring the security, resilience and availability of our most critical war fighting assets remains a top priority," the Air Force spokesperson said. When reached by CBS News, Leidos, the tech company which has served as the main contractor operating Cloud One since May, declined to comment specifically on the hack, deferring to the Air Force. A Leidos spokesperson noted that earlier this year, it announced a $454.9 million contract to modernize and secure the Air Force's cloud operations.The alleged incident follows a series of breaches and outages that have been reported at federal agencies this month, including at the National Security Agency, the CIA, the FBI, the U.S. Department of Agriculture, and the Federal Aviation Administration, the latter of which prompted a nationwide ground stop that triggered chaos for tens of thousands of travelers at U.S. airports.In the FBI breach reported last week, hackers accessed a large database used by law enforcement agencies nationwide to access criminal records. The NSA's network outage was linked to an urgent patching of vulnerabilities in PHP, the programming language that powers the majority of all websites, multiple sources told CBS News. The NSA's internal network, which is used to store and share classified information, went offline during the ordeal, the sources said. The CIA and Office of the Director of National Intelligence, meanwhile, suffered an intrusion of an internal network that gathers intelligence from publicly available information, such as social media. An ODNI official told CBS News in a statement Tuesday that there were "no disruptions to critical capabilities or classified systems" from that breach. national.body: There were no injuries when the wingtips of two American Airlines jets made contact Friday evening on the tarmac of Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport outside Washington, D.C., officials said. American Airlines Flight 638 clipped the wing of American Airlines Flight 2152 a little after 5 p.m. local time while both aircraft were taxiing for departure, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. In a separate statement provided to CBS News, American Airlines said that both planes returned to their gates and were "removed from service for inspection by our maintenance team."Both the FAA and American Airlines said no injuries were reported.The Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority said in a statement that its fire and rescue personnel responded to both planes. The airports authority said there were no disruptions to any other flights.Flight 638 was bound for Dallas, while Flight 2152 was headed to Chicago. The airline said passengers would be placed on new planes and depart for their destinations later Friday night. Earlier this month, two passengers suffered minor injuries when the wingtip of a Copa Airlines jet struck the nose of a UPS cargo plane on the tarmac of Miami International Airport. And in early October, the left wingtip of a Delta Air Lines plane clipped the tail of an Air Canada aircraft on the tarmac of Los Angeles International Airport. There were no injuries. Reagan Airport has three runways, one of which is considered the busiest in the nation, and it operates with a tightly restricted airspace due to its location near the White House and Capitol Hill. In January 2025, an Army Black Hawk helicopter collided in midair with an American Airlines plane that was approaching to land at Reagan Airport. All 64 people aboard the American Airlines flight were killed, along with the three soldiers aboard the chopper.

national.title: 'Poison seller' Kenneth Law apologises in court to the families of his victims
national.summary: The Canadian man, who pleaded guilty to 14 counts of aiding and abetting suicide earlier this year, said he was remorseful for his actions.
national.body:
The Canadian man who sold toxic chemicals through online suicide forums in 40 countries apologised in court to the families of the victims, saying he deeply regrets his actions and will never repeat them.

Kenneth Law made the remarks on Friday during a sentencing hearing where prosecutors asked a judge to give him a 25-year prison term.

The 61-year-old pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding the suicide deaths of 14 people in Ontario, Canada, though he has admitted to causing the deaths of dozens of victims in England and Wales.

He will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths under a plea deal which saw Canadian authorities withdraw more serious charges of murder.

During Friday's sentencing hearing in an Ontario court, prosecutors stressed that many of his victims were young and struggling with mental distress.

If Law receives the prosecution's recommended sentence, he would serve just under 20 years in prison, after accounting for credit for time served since his May 2023 arrest.

As she sought to make her case in court on Friday, Crown Attorney Kathleen Doherty described Law as a predator taking advantage of "vulnerable people".

"What they needed was help. But what they found was Mr Law and his products for death," Doherty said.

national.title: Two American Airlines planes clip wings before takeoff at Reagan airport in 'tense' moment
national.summary: No injuries were reported, and the FAA plans to investigate the incident, which occurred during taxiing.
national.body:
Two American Airlines jets hit each other at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport while taxiing for departure in Washington DC.

One jet "clipped the wing" of the other at around 5:10 ET (22:10) on Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement. No injuries were reported, and the FAA plans to investigate.

Both aircraft returned to the gate and were removed from service to be inspected by maintenance teams, American Airlines said.

The incident happened at the same airport where 67 people died in a deadly collision between a jetliner and an Army helicopter in January 2025.

"American Airlines Flight 638 clipped the wing of American Airlines Flight 2152 while taxiing for departure," the FAA said.

Air traffic controllers can be heard on an audio recording saying two Boeing 737s clipped wings on the airport's runway. The controllers requested an emergency response and fire personnel to the plane, then directed the aircraft to return to the gate.

The "wingtips of both Boeing 737-800s made contact," American Airlines said in a statement. The airline added that it is working to get affected passengers who were evacuated from both planes to their destinations as soon as possible.

A passenger on flight 2152 headed to Chicago, O'Hare airport, told the BBC that he felt a "large jolt" on the right side of the aircraft as they were taxiing before departure. The other plane, flight 638, was bound for Dallas-Fort Worth airport.

national.title: The Indian 'Tamasha queen' whose fans paid for a show that never happened
national.summary: A new Bollywood flim spotlights the remarkable life of dancer and singer Vithabhai Narayangaonkar.
national.body:
Few things could keep Vithabai Narayangaonkar, one of the greatest stars of Maharashtra's folk theatre, away from the stage.

In the 1960s, the singer, dancer and troupe leader was performing in Shikhar Shingnapur, a village in the western Indian state, when she went into labour.

"She quietly stepped behind the stage into a makeshift tent while the rest of us continued performing," her daughter, veteran folk artist Mangala Bansode, told BBC Marathi.

Outside, the restless audience kept shouting: "Where is Vitha?"

When Vithabai returned to the stage, she was cradling her newborn son, the seventh of her eight children.

"The audience was stunned, but they quietly left, saying, 'We will watch your performance later'," Bansode recalled.

Outspoken and quick-witted, Vithabai held audiences across Maharashtra in thrall for decades, earning the title of Tamasha Samradnyi – the empress of Tamasha, the state's traditional travelling folk theatre.

Now, more than two decades after her death, her life has inspired a Bollywood musical, Eetha, starring Shraddha Kapoor, and due for release on 4 December.

national.body: Heavy rain over flooded East Coast communities began easing Friday, and power was slowly restored to hundreds of thousands of customers as some places stayed on guard for high-tide flooding following a round of holiday storms.The storms snarled travel and downed trees and power lines. The heavy weather led to water rescues from New York to Virginia. In New York City, preparations were underway to hold Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade on Saturday after an unprecedented postponement because of rain and high winds.Elsewhere, wet snow fell as far south as the Tennessee Valley and freezing rain moved across northern New England. Cold rain was reported in parts of the Midwest, including the Ohio Valley and the lower Great Lakes.Another storm system in the Northwest brought rain along coastal Oregon. More snow was forecast in the Cascade Range and in mountain passes in Montana and Wyoming.There were 2,893 flights in the U.S. delayed as of Friday afternoon, with another 151 canceled, according to the flight tracking service FlightAware.The number of power outages, which peaked Thursday at more than 900,000 customers, fell by approximately 50% by Friday afternoon to under 400,000, according to utility tracker PowerOutage.us. Of those, about 90,000 were in Pennsylvania. national.title: A clinic is reassessing people with ADHD and autism diagnoses - but critics fear it could deepen stigma
national.summary: While many people find a diagnosis for ADHD or autism affirming, a government-funded clinic in Sweden is re-assessing people who feel it does not reflect them.
national.body:
Freya looks nervous as she walks into a psychiatric clinic in Sweden for an ADHD assessment.

Countries around the world have seen a huge increase in ADHD diagnoses over recent decades. For many people this can be life changing, helping them understand themselves better and access support.

But Freya (not her real name) is not attending a long-awaited appointment to secure a diagnosis.

This government-funded clinic offers autism and ADHD diagnosis reassessments - its doctors believe it is the first in the world dedicated solely to this purpose.

At 12, Freya was struggling with anxiety at school and sought out professional help. "They thought I had ADHD," she says.

But as she grew up, she felt that she did not experience ADHD symptoms. "I don't think I had it in the first place," she now says.

Her doubts about the diagnosis became more pressing as a teenager, when she discovered that in Sweden, it could be a barrier to pursuing her dream career of joining the police.

"I want to have every option open," she tells BBC World Service.

national.summary: Nancy Preston, a veteran, helped aspiring food entrepreneurs start their own businesses after her time in the U.S. military. She shares her Brief But Spectacular take on finding new ways to serve.
national.body: Nancy Preston, a veteran, helped aspiring food entrepreneurs start their own businesses after her time in the U.S. military. She shares her Brief But Spectacular take on finding new ways to serve. Nick Schifrin: And finally from us: It is the season of thanks. Nancy Preston is a veteran, and after her time in the U.S. military, she helped aspiring food entrepreneurs start their own businesses. She shares her Brief But Spectacular take on finding new ways to serve. Nancy Preston: I joined the Army because I didn't have a lot of other opportunities. I knew I wanted to go to college at some point, and I knew I would need money, which I didn't have. The Army was going to provide me $12,000, which it was called the Montgomery G.I. Bill at time. So I took the opportunity to go. I was deployed to Iraq for 15 months. We were part of the summer surge. My unit was 3rd Armored, 3rd Infantry Division. And we were responsible for winning the hearts and minds of the Iraqi people in the eastern part of Iraq. When I came out of the Army, it's very common that hiring managers don't translate or understand your experiences. And it was just like that for me. I think a lot of veterans do end up being underemployed or unemployed because both the employer doesn't understand how great their experience is, and the veteran sometimes doesn't understand how great his or her experience is. The DOD is the largest employer in the world. For the hiring managers to not understand this giant sector that employs so many people is a bit of a shame. But I was very lucky. I went into a company where they actually hire veterans. And so that's what it was at USAA. They actually knew how to read my C.V. When I got out of the Army, I founded Milk Money Kitchens. We are an on-demand shared kitchen facility where we rent to food entrepreneurs kitchen space by the hour or more to help food entrepreneurs launch and grow in New York City. I only hire for underserved communities. I think about Sergeant Bowen (ph), who took me to the education center and said, take these tests. I think you have potential. I left the Army, but I found that I never left service. Most veterans do continue service, and they do continue just wanting to help people. My name is Nancy Preston, and this is my Brief But Spectacular take on finding new ways to serve.

national.title: Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out
national.summary: China's immense clout now also has the flex of soft power. Critics and dissidents say their voices are being drowned out.
national.body:
For Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa, who has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades, the thinning of the crowds is the clearest measure of how much his cause is slipping off the world's radar.

"Back in 2018, we could easily get thousands of people out in the streets to protest against China's human rights violations. Nowadays, we have trouble finding even 500."

It was in 2018 that reports emerged that China had detained up to a million Uyghurs and other Muslims in mass internment camps in its north-western province of Xinjiang. Beijing, which said the camps were for "re-education" to counter separatist violence, denied the allegations detailing alarming rights abuses.

But an international outcry, including protests, followed. Western governments rolled out trade bans and sanctions against senior Chinese officials, and froze their assets, and at least nine countries issued parliamentary resolutions condemning the detentions.

It was a time "when we felt the world was finally listening", says Dolkun, 59, who served as president of the Munich-based World Uyghur Congress from 2017-2024 .

But today, "we find ourselves competing against economic interests and geopolitical calculations to capture the world's attention. For me, this is one of the most painful aspects of our struggle".

Few corners of the world remain untouched by China's rise. Its electric vehicles pack highways from Brazil to Belgium, made-in-China batteries, solar panels, AI models and microdramas fuel daily consumption in so many places, and Labubu dolls , Pop Mart's furry gap-toothed plush, dangle from backpacks almost everywhere.

China's immense economic clout now also has the flex of soft power , drowning out voices that say their fight against the Communist Party cannot compete with the country's gleaming skylines, advanced exports or futuristic ambitions.

national.title: Hundreds of thousands still without power a day after US slammed with Thanksgiving storms
national.summary: Pennsylvania and neighbouring states remain badly affected on Friday after both coasts were lashed with wind and rain.
national.body:
Hundreds of thousands of people are without power after severe weather hit both coasts of the United States during the Thanksgiving holiday.

Eastern areas were lashed on Thursday by a powerful storm which brought high winds, heavy rain and coastal flooding. Pennsylvania remained the state worst hit by power cuts early on Friday, according to monitoring site Poweroutage.us.

Conditions are now improving, though forecasters caution that it will take some time. The West Coast also was affected by its own storms.

Flight disruption persisted, too, with hundreds more delays and cancellations reported on Friday - another busy travel day.

More than 2,700 flights within, into, or out of the US were delayed and nearly 150 cancelled on Friday.

On Thanksgiving, more than 2,500 US flights were delayed and more than 450 were cancelled, according to Flightaware.com. One passenger told the BBC he had been stuck at New York's LaGuardia Airport for 13 hours while trying to fly to see friends in Chicago for Thanksgiving.

Beyond the travel disruption, impacts were widespread across the East Coast, and US President Donald Trump said he would consider releasing emergency funds.

Bridges closed in Maryland due to severe winds, while waves battered beaches in Delaware as water seeped onto the boardwalk. On the wettest Thanksgiving on record in Washington, tidal waters surged and soaked runways at Reagan Washington National Airport.

national.title: OpenAI countersues Apple over allegations of stealing trade secrets
national.summary: OpenAI alleged in a lawsuit Friday that Apple sets up departing employees to be accused of stealing trade secrets.
national.body: OpenAI on Friday responded to Apple's June lawsuit accusing the company of stealing trade secrets by countersuing. The ChatGPT maker alleged that Apple sets up departing employees to be accused of stealing proprietary information. Apple created "a situation in which it can accuse virtually any departing employee, and their new employer, of 'stealing' purported Apple trade secrets," the suit, filed in the Northern District of California, claims. In a statement provided to CBS News Friday, an Apple spokesperson said that the case "is about OpenAI employees deliberately stealing, accessing, and using Apple's secret and confidential information regarding our unreleased technologies, processes, and products — not about inadvertent retention of Apple information. OpenAI's counterclaims are a transparent attempt to distract from the substance of Apple's lawsuit, in which OpenAI has already been ordered to stop using Apple's confidential information."Apple's complaint in June accused OpenAI and two of its employees, Chief Hardware Officer Tang Tan and Chang Liu, a technical staffer at the company, of stealing Apple's proprietary information to help OpenAI develop its own hardware. Both formerly worked at Apple. OpenAI claims in its countersuit Friday that Apple's employment practices are designed to set a trap for a departing employee and their future employer — "a trap that can be sprung whenever Apple sees an opportunity to slow down a potential competitor."Tech analysts expect OpenAI to make a foray into hardware design, putting it in more direct competition with Apple. In July 2025, OpenAI acquired the AI device startup of former Apple star designer Jony Ive, io Products Inc.

national.body:
Alejandro Granadillo, Associated Press Alejandro Granadillo, Associated Press

SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico (AP) — Thousands of people protested Friday in Puerto Rico's capital as anger and frustration erupted over record high electric rates, the surging cost of living, deterioration in basic services and other issues.

Retirees, university students, bus drivers and others joined the protest organized by some 30 groups ranging from unions to religious organizations. The crowds gathered in front of the largest mall in the Caribbean on Black Friday for what organizers dubbed the "Day of National Outrage."

Hundreds of demonstrators arrived by bus in San Juan from dozens of cities and towns across the island.

WATCH: Drought and aging infrastructure plunge Puerto Rico into a water crisis

Asked what problems Puerto Rico had, 74-year-old Radamés García Badillo said "Where to start? The outrage is absolute."

He noted that power and water services are unreliable, with his neighborhood going dark at least once a week for several hours.

"We're buying less because things are extremely expensive," he said. "For us retirees, it is essential to make every dollar stretch."

national.title: Spanish PM and rivals rally supporters in final pitch for votes
national.summary: Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez wants to defy the polls, and his main rivals accuse him of not telling the truth and of "betrayal".
national.body:
Spain's main party leaders have held their final rallies ahead of Sunday's election, with Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez saying he is confident of defying the polls.

"I cannot imagine us losing," he said, posing for selfies with supporters in red T-shirts and accusing conservative rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo of planning a coalition with the far right.

Feijóo's People's Party (PP) is narrowly ahead in the polls, and in the final hours of the campaign he travelled first to Barcelona and then Seville, promising voters a new political era of "truth, decency and good governance".

He accused Sánchez of evading questions on key issues like corruption, rail disasters, immigration and the national debt.

The Socialist leader heads one of Europe's few left-wing governments, and with the French presidential elections five months away, there is a real chance that two of the continent's biggest economies could move to the right in quick succession.

Almost 39 million people have a vote in Spain and while commentators expect a high turnout, most polls have suggested a close finish. Under Spanish electoral law, no polls have been published since Monday.

"This time, yes, we're going to do it," Feijóo told PP supporters, in a nod to his failure to form a government three years ago despite winning most seats.

If he gets to form a government this time, it will be with the support of anti-immigration party Vox, led by Santiago Abascal, whose final rally took place in front of thousands of people in a bull-ring in Valencia on Spain's east coast.

national.title: Mexico's government is slamming a DEA crime tip line as foreign interference. Others are thrilled.
national.summary: The announcement opened the latest chapter in an ongoing struggle between the U.S. and Mexican governments over who has the right to take action against cartels in Mexico.
national.body:
Fabiola Sanchez, Associated Press Fabiola Sanchez, Associated Press

MEXICO CITY (AP) — The government in Mexico is railing against the U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency's anonymous tip line for reports against criminals and corrupt officials in the Latin American nation, slamming it as foreign interference.

In the state of Sinaloa, journalist Juan Manuel Partida Valdez was among the first to write to the WhatsApp line on Thursday, just a day after DEA chief Terry Cole called for anonymous reports on his X account.

The announcement opened the latest chapter in an ongoing struggle between the U.S. and Mexican governments over who has the right to take action against cartels in Mexico.

Partida Valdez, president of the Sinaloa Journalists Association, said he sent information about alleged ties between Sinaloa politicians and criminal groups because authorities have failed to put an end to violence and corruption that has bled his northern Mexican region dry in recent years.

"I talk to so many people — in the streets, on social media, on WhatsApp and in chats — and you realize what people think: We're all fed up," the 67-year-old told The Associated Press on Friday. "We're fed up with narco-governments."

On Friday, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said she escalated her fight with Washington over the tip line, filing a formal complaint with the U.S. Embassy for interfering in Mexico's internal affairs.

"We have made it very clear in our relationship with the United States that the relationship is one of coordination, not subordination," Sheinbaum said in her morning press briefing.

national.title: 25-year sentence sought for former chef who aided 14 suicides
national.summary: Kenneth Law pleaded guilty earlier this year to aiding 14 suicides in Canada, but he has admitted to selling his so-called suicide kits globally.
national.body: Canadian prosecutors on Friday requested a 25-year prison sentence for a man who sold poison to help people die by suicide, stressing his victims were largely young and experiencing mental distress. Former chef Kenneth Law pleaded guilty earlier this year to aiding 14 suicides in Canada, but he has admitted to selling his so-called suicide kits globally through a series of online forums. Prosecutors had also charged him with murder but, citing a lack of evidence, agreed to withdraw the more serious accusations in exchange for Law pleading guilty to lesser offenses. That decision drew widespread condemnation, notably from friends and family of victims who believed Law was directly responsible for killing their loved ones, but prosecutors maintained they would still seek a stiff penalty. "An appropriate global sentence to impose in this matter is 25 years less (time already served)," Crown prosecutor Katie Doherty told the court. Courts often use comparable cases in determining sentencing, but Doherty noted there is "no case even remotely similar to Mr Law's conduct." The Canadian public was shocked when the breadth of Law's operation was revealed following his arrest. He sold poison to people in at least 41 countries, including China, France, and Brazil. He sold 330 packages to people in the United Kingdom, according to an agreed statement of facts signed by the defense and prosecution. There, 79 deaths are linked to him, according to Canadian prosecutors. national.title: Canada's Supreme Court largely upholds a Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
national.summary: The 2019 law, known as Bill 21, bans religious symbols — including Muslim headscarves, Sikh turbans, Jewish skullcaps and Christian crosses — for workers covered by it.
national.body:
TORONTO (AP) — Canada's Supreme Court on Friday upheld most of a Quebec law banning public schoolteachers, police officers and other public employees in positions of authority from wearing religious symbols at work. The ruling affirmed Quebec's power to override certain constitutional rights to keep the ban in place.

The 2019 law, known as Bill 21, bans religious symbols — including Muslim headscarves, Sikh turbans, Jewish skullcaps and Christian crosses — for workers covered by it.

Canada has long embraced multiculturalism, encouraging people to retain their cultural and religious identities. Supporters of Quebec's ban say public officials should avoid wearing religious symbols to demonstrate government neutrality.

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon welcomed the ruling as "a victory for secularism" and for Quebec's ability to make different choices from the rest of Canada.

The court upheld Quebec's use of the "notwithstanding clause," which allows lawmakers to override certain rights, including religious freedom and equality. Those rights are protected by the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, Canada's equivalent of the U.S. Bill of Rights. Lawmakers must renew the override every five years to keep it in effect.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said he respected the ruling but pledged that his government would not use the constitutional override. He stressed that constitutional rights are particularly important for minorities and vulnerable people.

"Canada is a mosaic," Carney said, adding that it represents more than different backgrounds and identities. "It's a commitment, in my judgment, a commitment to how we treat each other."

Carney also welcomed the court's finding that judges can still declare that a law violates constitutional rights even when the override allows it to remain in force. He said that scrutiny helps inform Canadians and is useful in a democracy.

national.title: Capsized tanker carrying 7,000 tonnes of diesel to be towed away from Ibiza
national.summary: There are fears of a major oil spillage off Ibiza but the ship's fuel tanks are so far intact.
national.body:
A tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel which capsized off the holiday island of Ibiza on Thursday will be towed to the port of Cartagena, officials in Spain say.

All 17 of the Malta-registered Med Emre's crew members were rescued but the chief engineer later died in hospital. Six people were treated for minor injuries.

There had been concerns of a major oil spillage in the western Mediterranean but an inspection showed that the ship's fuel tanks are intact. An investigation is under way into what happened.

The vessel had been travelling from Algeciras near Gibraltar to Barcelona and is expected to arrive in Cartagena on Monday in what is being seen as a challenging rescue operation.

In a statement on Friday, the Spanish transport ministry said the tanker would be towed to Cartagena "as it is the only one [port] that meets the technical requirements to carry out cargo extraction and repair work".

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez told Cadena SER radio network he hoped the tanker could be taken to port "in the coming hours, in the coming days".

"The information suggests that, indeed... this leak is not happening", he added.

The Spanish authorities provided no details about how the diesel would be extracted.

national.summary: So far, the EPA said there has continued to be "zero" airborne lead detected in the region since Wednesday's controlled detonation. While that's reassuring, residents and some elected officials have criticized the Army for not being more transparent and providing more notice when it first determined
national.body:
Susan Montoya Bryan, Associated Press Susan Montoya Bryan, Associated Press

The detonation of the nation's aging stockpile of lead azide, which spurred widespread concerns about potential environmental contamination, has been deemed a success by the U.S. Army. But questions remain about how and when the federal government communicated its plans.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency said about 300 people spent Thursday in the field sampling schools, playgrounds, churches and homes across the region. Results were expected in the coming days.

More than 1,500 samples were taken of air, water, soil and dust before the detonation. After, they took hundreds of samples including from homes, parks and drinking water, the EPA has said.

WATCH: What the Army's Iowa detonation means for nearby communities

So far, the EPA said there has continued to be "zero" airborne lead detected in the region since Wednesday's controlled detonation.

While that's reassuring, residents and some elected officials have criticized the Army for not being more transparent and providing more notice when it first determined the stockpile was unstable.

A notice that plant managers planned to neutralize the stockpile was posted on a government website. Growing concern led to a plant closure in March that was publicized, and an October public meeting warned that the chemicals would soon need to be detonated.

national.title: Marching bands scramble to cover NYC costs after parade rearranged
national.summary: Stormy weather in New York City prompted organisers to push back the Macy's parade by two days - leaving some musicians stuck.
national.body:
Since New York City officials postponed the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, a precaution ahead of a storm that brought heavy rain, wind and flooding, hundreds of touring performers who traveled from across the US to perform were thrust into chaos.

"It was jarring," said Ryan Demkovich, director of a Texas high school marching band. After learning the news, he had to scramble to make new arrangements for over 500 people.

Demkovich and his Pearland High School band made the quick decision to launch a fundraiser, reaching $350,000 (£267,000) in just a few hours.

Still, some performers reportedly had to skip the parade, a televised, traditional Thanksgiving event - now rescheduled for Saturday.

On Wednesday afternoon, a day before the event, organisers announced the postponement, in part due to concerns around the parade's giant balloons in strong winds.

The balloons, inflated on Wednesday, were then temporarily deflated - along with the spirits of those who journeyed to the city to watch the action.

The move represented the first time the event had been postponed in its 100-year history, although it was suspended altogether during World War II.

Each year, a number of marching bands travel from across the country, from high schools and colleges, to perform at the event. This is considered a huge opportunity, as the parade is watched by millions in person and on TV.

national.title: U.S. military says it disabled another ship that tried to breach naval blockade on Iranian ports
national.summary: A military aircraft fired "precision munitions" at the stern of the Palau-flagged M/V Pacific Archer on Thursday, and the "ship's propulsion was ultimately disabled and the civilian crew was unharmed," U.S. Central Command said in a statement.
national.body:
Konstantin Toropin, Associated Press Konstantin Toropin, Associated Press

WASHINGTON (AP) — The U.S. military has disabled a merchant ship in the Gulf of Oman that was trying to run its blockade of Iranian ports, U.S. Central Command said Friday.

A military aircraft fired "precision munitions" at the stern of the Palau-flagged M/V Pacific Archer on Thursday, and the "ship's propulsion was ultimately disabled and the civilian crew was unharmed," it said in a statement.

According to U.S. Central Command, the Pacific Archer left the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas before it attempted to run the blockade. Ship tracking websites list the vessel's destination as Singapore.

WATCH: 'We will not allow that to happen,' Trump says of reported Iran dirty bomb threat

The commander of the Iranian navy, Shahram Irani, said Friday on state television that Iran will carry out operations "that will not only break the naval blockade but also drive the enemy out of the region's waters."

The strike comes as the Trump administration weighs its options in the long-simmering war with Iran, which began at the end of February and has settled into a quiet stalemate in the past several months.

Earlier in November, officials in the region told The Associated Press that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was pushing the U.S. to restart the war or allow Israel to launch airstrikes on Iran's nuclear facilities and missile capabilities.

President Claudia Sheinbaum said Friday the country's foreign ministry has lodged a formal complaint with U.S. Ambassador Ron Johnson."We have made it very clear in our relationship with the United States that the relationship is one of coordination, not subordination," she said in her daily news briefing. Sheinbaum, in harsh comments Thursday, read excerpts from a new investigation by The Associated Press revealing how the DEA allowed at least 1.4 million counterfeit fentanyl pills to go unseized as it spent eight months tracking a drug trafficking ring flooding the Southwest with deadly drugs. "The DEA has plenty of work to do in its own country. A lot," Sheinbaum said, pointing to the AP report. "The first thing it should do is investigate corruption in the United States linked to organized crime, or what they call terrorist groups.""It's clearly an act of interference," Sheinbaum added. Imagine, she mused, if Mexico "opened a WhatsApp service for reporting corruption in the United States. How would the U.S. government view that?" Officials said they were following up on leads she may have taken public transportation and were checking Greyhound buses and Amtrak trains.The U.S. Marshals Service is offering a $5,000 reward for information leading to her arrest.Taylor is about 5-foot-7 and 180 pounds and has blue eyes and red hair. Authorities are asking anyone who sees her to call 911.All prison facilities in New Mexico were put on lockdown in the wake of the escape as a precaution. That lockdown was lifted at 6 a.m. on Friday.

national.title: Using a drone and a poop-sniffing dog, scientists perform health checks on endangered orcas
national.summary: In their search for their dwindling food source, the whales are spending less time in the Salish Sea, the maze of inland waters between Washington State and British Columbia.
national.body:
Manuel Valdes, Associated Press Manuel Valdes, Associated Press

KINGSTON, Wash. (AP) — Every fall for the last few years, Deborah Giles starts her work day with one question in mind: Where are the orcas?

Giles is tracking the Southern Resident killer whales, an endangered species whose population recovery is faltering despite years of protection. In their search for their dwindling food source, the whales are spending less time in the Salish Sea, the maze of inland waters between Washington State and British Columbia. But in the last half-decade, the orcas have been hunting coho and chum salmon just north of Seattle during the fall.

It's providing an opportunity for collaboration between The SeaDoc Society and the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance. They're using drones mounted with petri dishes and microscope slides to collect droplets from whale spouts and employing a poop-sniffing dog to find stool samples, providing much-needed wellness checks for as many of the 76 remaining whales as they can find.

"They were here before us, long before us," said Giles. "They're a group of animals that are uniquely bonded to this place and to each other."

A research drone flown by Dr. James Sheppard of the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance hovers over K33 "Tika," a Southern Resident killer whale, while attempting to collect breath samples, on Puget Sound near Possession Point State Park, Washington, on Nov. 18, 2026. Photo by Lindsey Wasson/AP (NMFS/NOAA permit #26288-01)

Before colonization of the Pacific Northwest, the orca's main prey — Chinook salmon — could weigh more than 100 pounds (45.36 kilograms) and their numbers were abundant along the West Coast, Giles said.

But when American settlers came to the region, they built dams and overfished salmon. As cities and ports grew, boats created more noise, hindering the orca's hunting. Toxic chemicals flowed into sea water. And Chinook salmon now average about 12.5 pounds (5.66 kilograms), Giles said.

national.title: Weary of war but with no sign of backing down, Kyiv faces another punishing winter
national.summary: Ukraine settles in for another devastating winter as the questions persists: how will it all end?
national.body:
Something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight. It's not really for phones - it seems to be part of a wider strategy to disorient the missiles and drones the Russians are sending over.

Aside from little things like that, though, Kyiv seems fairly normal at first sight. You become well aware there's a war on when sirens begin to wail and people check their phones for the notifications which tell them there's a red alert and missiles are on their way. You can even buy gadgets that show you which direction the drones are coming from, and what type they are.

The drones and ballistic missiles have been hitting in sizeable numbers over the last couple of weeks. On the morning of Monday 16 November, the battle of the bridges began. Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge which links Russia to illegally occupied Crimea. Then it launched a bigger wave of missiles and drones, damaging the central road-bridge arch. A few hours later, presumably in revenge, Russia fired seven ballistic missiles at Kyiv, disabling two of the nine bridges that cross the River Dnipro.

The war has dragged on for more than four and a half years, killing what some estimate could be 100,000 Ukrainian troops and 18,000 Ukrainian civilians, according to the United Nations, and probably more. Its infrastructure, too, has been battered, as well as its morale. While temperatures drop to freezing at night, and with Ukrainians regularly suffering from no light, heat or water thanks to Russian strikes, can the country survive another difficult winter under bombardment? And what would a peace deal, if one could be struck, look like?

Kyiv is mostly dark at night, thanks to Russia's campaign of targeting Ukraine's electricity generating capability. In the blackness last week, the air raid sirens started wailing across the city, and our hotel's warning announcements came over the loudspeakers. Within a few minutes, we heard the first explosions. I jumped out of bed and stared out of the window into the darkness. After a few seconds two more missiles landed, lighting up the entire sky momentarily in a blaze of white and red. They were uncomfortably close.

Many people prefer to go to the shelters when there's a red alert. Others just stay in bed and hope the law of averages will protect them. It usually does. During one of the heaviest attacks last week, the number of fatalities was in single figures.

national.title: A Ukraine loan is in limbo after EU budget talks stall. Leaders will try again
national.summary: The spending package is small compared to national budgets — around 1% to 1.2% of gross national income — but it encapsulates the ambitions of the world's biggest trading bloc and how it sees itself on the international stage.
national.body:
BRUSSELS (AP) — After struggling to chaperone Europe's leaders through more than 12 hours of high-stakes budget negotiations, European Council President António Costa faced reporters early Friday with a stark assessment. "We didn't reach an agreement," he said.

Government leaders from the 27-nation European Union failed to narrow down the size of the 2028-2034 budget — let alone how it might be used. An important loan for Ukraine was caught up in the wrangling.

The spending package is small compared to national budgets — around 1% to 1.2% of gross national income — but it encapsulates the ambitions of the world's biggest trading bloc and how it sees itself on the international stage.

Costa said "some member states asked for further reductions" in how much they would have to pay in, according to his latest proposals, while most were "opposed to further cuts, and some even proposed to reverse some cuts."

It was a day of brinksmanship that saw the leaders playing tough for national audiences.

In three weeks, they will try again. The stakes are high. Elections in some key countries are approaching, and new hardline governments or shaky coalitions could complicate matters further.

In coming days, Costa will draw his conclusions from the summit talks — held in two plenary sessions, several group meetings, and the corridor conversations that typify EU budget negotiations — and consult again with capitals.

Some leaders, notably from countries that pay more into the budget than they get back in allocations, skipped certain meetings. But Costa, a former Portuguese prime minister, was unruffled.

national.summary: Ukraine's president voices frustration with US and says it is not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks to end the war.
national.body:
Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives.

In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president complained the US was not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks, and called it "strange" that Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Putin.

"Of course it's up to the president of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.

"He's an aggressor, and a killer... He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.

Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the US.

Trump's two envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.

Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, said on Wednesday that Putin had shown "restraint" by not using nuclear weapons in Ukraine. He also described Putin as a "grand master of politics".

The latest round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this month made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.

national.title: Kenyan doomsday cult leader convicted over further 123 deaths
national.summary: Paul Mackenzie is found guilty of killing his followers, weeks after being jailed for the mass murder of children.
national.body:
A court in Kenya has convicted the leader of a doomsday Christian cult of the manslaughter of 123 of his followers.

Paul Mackenzie was found guilty in Mombasa of ordering his followers, all adults, to fast to death in Shakahola forest near the coast between January 2021 and September 2023.

Earlier this month Mackenzie was jailed for 200 years for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children, in the same mass killing.

Mackenzie had pleaded not guilty to manslaughter and one of his lawyers said he would appeal against the conviction after sentencing, Reuters news agency reports.

Warning: This article contains details which some people might find distressing.

The court also convicted 29 others including Mackenzie's wife, Rhoda Mumbua Maweu, of their part in the manslaughter.

Sixty defendants were acquitted. The Director of Public Prosecutions indicated that an appeal would be launched against their acquittal.

The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest, near the Indian Ocean coast.

Caleb Williams put the Chicago Bears in first place. Joe Milton III put a dagger in his former team's season. Tyler Bass put the Buffalo Bills in position for a No. 1 seed.

Making his third career start with his third team in his third NFL season, Milton was 21 of 31 for 331 yards, three TDs, one interception, one TD run and a 121.8 passer rating.

After the defense sacked Dak Prescott on a fourth down, Milton completed two passes for 14 yards and Jake Elliott drilled a 59-yard field goal with 2 seconds remaining. Milton was signed by Philadelphia off Dallas' practice squad last month after Jalen Hurts was placed on injured reserve.

The Eagles (4-7) have won two in a row to keep their slim playoff hopes alive in an NFC East led by the New York Giants (6-3-1). national.title: Canada's top court largely upholds Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
national.summary: The law faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their fundamental rights.
national.body:
Canada's top court has largely upheld a Quebec law banning public sector workers from wearing religious symbols, including the hijab and the cross.

The law, known as Bill 21, faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their fundamental rights.

Quebec passed the law in 2019 under a unique fixture of Canada's constitution called the "notwithstanding clause" - a legal loophole that allows governments to override certain rights, like freedom of religion.

The Supreme Court's decision is one of the most closely watched in Canadian history, with an impact that will be felt both in Quebec and across the country.

Reacting to the ruling on CBC, Prime Minister Mark Carney said his government would study its implications, adding it was important for all legislatures "to respect the rights and liberties of all Canadians, including those in the minority."

The Supreme Court was asked to weigh in on a number of questions, including on the constitutionality of Bill 21, whether Quebec's use of the notwithstanding clause was appropriate, and whether there are limits to its use.

On Friday, the top court confirmed the validity of Bill 21, but ruled that the law infringes on democratic rights by banning Quebec's elected officials from wearing a face covering for religious reasons.

The court also ruled that a Canadian court has the power to declare whether a law is consistent with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms even if the notwithstanding clause is invoked, but that they would not do so in this case.

national.title: Republicans rethink tariffs, giving Democrats an opening to challenge Trump
national.summary: After devastating election losses that centered on rising costs, many Republicans said they're open to reconsidering some of the levies that have become a central plank of Trump's global trade agenda.
national.body:
Steven Sloan, Associated Press Steven Sloan, Associated Press

Kevin Freking, Associated Press Kevin Freking, Associated Press

WASHINGTON (AP) — Democrats hoping to blunt President Donald Trump's tariffs when they retake control of Congress may find partners in an unlikely place: among his fellow Republicans.

After devastating election losses that centered on rising costs, many Republicans said they're open to reconsidering some of the levies that have become a central plank of Trump's global trade agenda. The administration proposed new tariffs on Wednesday targeting China, the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and nine other major trading partners.

WATCH: How Trump's newest tariffs could impact Americans and the economy

Whether Republicans actually buck Trump on tariffs could signal if election losses and the president's lame duck status shake what has been nearly lockstep fealty to him.

In interviews with more than a half dozen congressional Republicans since the election, most said they were open to reviewing tariffs, at least on a case-by-case basis. They expressed a desire for predictability and said Congress could reclaim its constitutional authority over tariffs. They were reluctant, however, to broadly curb the president's own tariff powers and acknowledged Trump could veto any repeal legislation.

But for Democrats eager to score some early bipartisan wins, the mere willingness of Republicans to revisit some tariffs could create an opening.

local.summary: VESTAL – Undefeated Dolgeville had rarely been tested on its way to a spot in Friday’s Class D West Semifinal at Dick Hoover Stadium. Randolph pushed the Blue Devils to the brink. But despite losing their starting quarterback to a broken collarbone on the third play of the game and losing the turnov
local.body:
VESTAL - Undefeated Dolgeville had rarely been tested on its way to a spot in Friday's Class D West Semifinal at Dick Hoover Stadium.

But despite losing their starting quarterback to a broken collarbone on the third play of the game and losing the turnover battle 3-0, the Section III champions found a way.

Dolgeville scored a pair of fourth-quarter touchdowns, stopped both of the Cardinals' drives in overtime and then scored a touchdown on second-and-goal from the 5-yard line on its second possession of overtime to beat the Section VI champions 20-14 in a New York State Public High School Athletic Association semifinal at Vestal High School.

"The kids didn't buckle," Dolgeville head coach Justin Daukontas said. "I'm very proud of them."

Now the Blue Devils - who have won 22 Section III championships - will look for their first state championship since 2000 when they take on Section I's Tuckahoe at 3 p.m. next Friday at Syracuse University's JMA Wireless Dome.

"The kids have worked tremendously hard. They set that goal back in June when we first met," Daukontas said. "That's the prize we've kept our eye on. I hope we can get it done Friday night."

For three quarters Friday in suburban Binghamton, Randolph looked like it might be making its first trip to a state final since 2014, taking a 14-0 lead despite being without its own starting quarterback Davion Johnson and being outgained by a wide margin.

"We came in Monday morning with a game plan and how we wanted to handle the quarterback situation," said Randolph head coach Nate Armella, who used both Alexander Garland and Carter Conley at quarterback. "They did a great job all week, but it's tough with just one week of practice and trying to give them two different looks at quarterback."

local.summary: Powerful winds and extensive ice have downed multiple power lines, leaving over 3,000 customers in Cattaraugus County without power.
local.body: Powerful winds and extensive ice have downed multiple power lines, leaving over 3,000 customers in Cattaraugus County without power.As of 3 p.m. on Friday, National Grid crews are continuing to clear downed lines, and 100 active outages are still being reported.According to the Cattaraugus County Office of Emergency Services, National Grid expects the majority of those customers will likely be without power until late this evening, although there are no official "ERTs" (estimated restoration times)."A lot of it was just being overwhelmed all at once," Farmersville EMS Captain Elizabeth Mann told WKBW. "We just kind of had to catch up and go from there." The Farmersville Fire Department has received 32 calls since 4:45 p.m. on Thursday."It just got cold, started raining, everything iced over, and all the trees started tipping over," Farmersville resident Daniel Koch Jr. recounted to WKBW. Koch's power remains out as well. "The refrigerator is getting warm. With the generator running, so that's where we're at.""Might take a trip to Olean," Koch said. "They got power over there," Koch said.While sympathetic to residents remaining in the dark, Mann encourages anyone in the affected areas to travel only if necessary."Trees are still coming down, and power lines are still coming down around us, so the more that you can stay indoors helps us be able to do our jobs better."The EMS captain added, "Definitely check on your elderly residents or elderly neighbors, family members, do the best you can to kind of check in on them, make sure that they have what they need, and stay indoors for the most part."Additionally, National Grid encourages everyone experiencing a power outage to contact their power company to report the outage. Even if your neighbor reported it or you see crews working in your area, still call to report and ensure your address is logged in their system. For National Grid customers, you can call 1-800-867-5222.This story is developing and will be updated when more information is made available.

A trailblazer in New York State government, Stewart-Cousins began her elected career as a
local.body:
State Gov. Kathy Hochul on Friday directed that flags on all State government buildings be flown at half-staff in honor of Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins, who passed away Thursday, Nov. 26, 2026.

A trailblazer in New York State government, Stewart-Cousins began her elected career as a Westchester County Legislator in 1996 before joining the State Senate in 2006. She made history in 2012 as the first woman to lead a legislative conference in New York State, and in 2019 made history again as the first woman and first Black woman to serve as Senate Majority Leader. Throughout her career, Stewart-Cousins championed civil rights, reproductive freedom and working families.

State Sen. George Borrello, R-Sunset Bay, issued this statement: "I was saddened to learn of the sudden passing of Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins. Her unexpected loss is a sad moment for the Senate, where she served with distinction for nearly two decades.

“The Majority Leader was a trailblazer who made history as the first woman to lead the New York State Senate. Beyond that historic achievement, she was a kind and gracious individual who treated everyone with dignity and respect.

“While we had very different political views and often disagreed on policy, I always appreciated her professionalism and civility. She never allowed those differences to affect the way she treated others.

“My sincere condolences go out to her children, grandchildren, family, friends and colleagues, as well as her dedicated staff. May she rest in peace."

local.title: State Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins has died
local.summary: She was the first woman and first African-American woman to serve as Senate Majority Leader, one of the most powerful positions in state government.
local.body:
State Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins, a Yonkers Democrat who made history as the first Black woman to lead a legislative conference in Albany, died unexpectedly on Friday. She was 76.

Stewart-Cousins’ longtime spokesperson, Mike Murphy, confirmed her death. The cause was not immediately clear.

Her passing comes less than two weeks after Senate Democrats voted to give her another two-year term as majority leader, one of the three most powerful positions in New York state government.

It sent shockwaves through the state Capitol, where Stewart-Cousins was a towering figure who played an outsize role in all substantial legislation that has passed since Democrats took control of the Senate in 2018.

“Andrea was more than just a remarkable public servant,” said Westchester County Executive Ken Jenkins, a longtime Stewart-Cousins ally. “She was a trailblazer, a dedicated advocate for the people of our county, and a leader whose impact will continue to be felt for generations.”

First elected to the Senate in 2006, Stewart-Cousins steadily rose through the ranks before her Democratic colleagues elected her minority leader in 2012.

Over time, she steadied what had been a tumultuous conference rocked by infighting and scandal. Under her watch, Democrats won enough seats over several election cycles to retake the Senate majority in 2018, knocking Republicans from the majority perch they had held for the better part of a century and making Stewart-Cousins the first woman to lead the Senate.

Since then, Stewart-Cousins was one of three people — along with the governor and Assembly Speaker Carl Heastie — to negotiate state budgets and major pieces of legislation. As leader, she helped pass bills to strengthen state abortion protections and reform the criminal-justice system, including a dramatic reduction in the number of crimes subject to cash bail.

local.title: THE GREAT OUTDOORS: Hunting memories
local.summary: My first memory of hunting was following my Dad around when he was hunting small game. I was around four years old and had a double-barreled “pop” shotgun. It didn’t shoot real shells like my Dad’s, but it made me…
local.body:
My first memory of hunting was following my Dad around when he was hunting small game. I was around four years old and had a double-barreled “pop” shotgun. It didn’t shoot real shells like my Dad’s, but it made me feel like a big hunter carrying it along as I followed him.

One day Dad spotted a deer at the end of a field we were hunting. He pointed it out to me and for a short period the deer stared at us. I, of course, didn’t know that the deer season was closed or that deer were a rare sight back then. I asked Dad if I could shoot at it and he said, “Aim high; she is a long way off.” When my toy gun popped she ran off and Dad said he thought my shot was low. I haven’t missed many deer since (although we sometimes have a tendency to forget misses) but that first “miss” with Dad will never be forgotten.

Doug Domedion, outdoorsman and nature photographer, resides in Medina. Contact him at 585-798-4022 or woodduck2020@yahoo.com .

Dear Annie: I’m 66 and in the final planning stages of my wedding. I was married to my first husband for 20 years and spent the decade after that single. local.title: Holley woman embraces her heritage and newfound sense of identity
local.summary: Bailey Kleckner discovered another part of her ancestry when she and her mother moved in with her maternal grandmother, a member of the Onondaga Turtle Clan.
local.body:
If you had asked Bailey Kleckner five years ago who Two Clawing Turtles was, she wouldn’t have known — even though it was her all along.

“My given name is Two Clawing Turtles,” the 18-year-old said. “And that is to represent my two-spirit identity and also my fierceness as I have grown into my higher sense of being.”

Sitting at a picnic table at a park in Holley, Orleans County, Kleckner looks relaxed as she reflects on her journey.

“It was about five years ago now that I moved out here to Holley,” Kleckner said. “My story of even knowing my heritage really didn't start until I moved out here.”

Kleckner grew up in Chili, where she sensed there was something about her ancestry she didn't fully understand. It wasn't until her parents separated and she and her mother moved in with her maternal grandmother, a member of the Onondaga Turtle Clan, that she began to discover that part of herself.

“Not knowing for so long, that was really life-changing,” Kleckner said of learning more about her Indigenous heritage. “It made me feel like I was finally at home.”

She later would go through the process to become an official member of the tribe.

The Onondaga Nation, one of the original five nations of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, bases membership on maternal lineage, according to Brad Powless, an Onondaga Nation council member.

World Wrestling Entertainment (WWE) star Bronson Reed has died.

The Australian-born professional wrestler, whose real name was Jermaine Haley, was just 38.

The WWE announced Reed’s death in a statement posted to Instagram Friday evening which read, “WWE is devastated to announce that Jermaine Haley, also known as Bronson Reed, passed away earlier today at the age of 38 due to medical complications.”

“Jermaine was a larger-than-life figure in WWE, but more importantly, he was a phenomenal person, a devoted family man, and a beloved colleague,” the statement continued.

The WWE concluded by saying, “Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Jermaine’s entire family, including his pregnant wife, Paige, their daughter, as well as all his friends, co-workers and fans.”

Born in Adelaide, South Australia, to a family of Samoan descent, Reed made his professional wrestling career in 2007 and his WWE debut in 2019.

entertainment.title: 5 NBC Dramas That Helped Define '80s Television
entertainment.summary: By the end of the 1980s, NBC had definitively planted its flag as one of the biggest names in television thanks to these dramas which defined the decade.
entertainment.body:
NBC Add TVLine on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover Shows like "Cheers" and "The Cosby Show" were some of NBC's most defining '80s sitcoms . The network began the decade lagging in its ratings, but by 1986 it dominated television, airing many of the most highly-rated shows of the time. These shows were part of historic shifts in television, but the change and success was not limited to sitcoms. During this iconic decade for television, NBC also aired some of its best dramas.

Led by network president Brandon Tartikoff from 1980 to 1991, NBC oversaw a complete shift in its dramatic programming. The genre welcomed excellent new aspects like serialized and realistic storytelling, larger casts, and bigger budgets. With wider character ensembles and overarching storylines, NBC aired some of the most groundbreaking and influential dramas of the decade.

Here is an unranked list of five of NBC's most defining dramas from the 1980s. While modern viewers may be accustomed to many of the aspects shared amongst the entries, audiences of the decade will never forget the change in television these shows signified.

The series focused on the officers of the Metropolitan Police Department's precinct on Hill Street, an urban area of an unnamed city. Led by Captain Frank Furillo (Daniel Travanti), the detectives and beat cops of the station navigated their tumultuous jobs while dealing with their own troubles.

By showcasing the cops' personal lives and shifting to serialized storytelling, "Hill Street Blues" paved the way for cop shows and television in general. Rather than fixed, idealistic portrayals of law enforcement, the 1980s ushered in a new era of gritty procedurals. It stands as one of the most iconic shows NBC aired during the decade, and also has one of the most recognizable opening theme songs.

The show centered on two detectives of the vice division of Miami's Metro-Dade Police Department. James Crockett (Don Johnson) and Ricardo Tubbs (Philip Michael Thomas) are partnered detectives who routinely work undercover to unravel illegal operations like drug and arms trafficking. It was created by Michael Mann (who also created "Crime Story" , an unfairly forgotten cop drama from the same decade).

Unlike the urban ruggedness and semi-realistic portrayals of cops in "Hill Street Blues," "Miami Vice" was focused on entertainment and high-octane action. As such, it was one of the most expensive television projects of the 1980s. The licensing for the music alone amounted to around $10,000 per episode.

entertainment.body:
Netflix Add TVLine on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover Warning: This article spoils the finale of "The Hunting Wives" Season 2 . Proceed at your own risk.

What a difference two years can make! The Season 2 finale of "The Hunting Wives," now streaming on Netflix, ends with a jaw-dropping time jump, revealing that Sophie and Margo's worst nightmares are still ahead of them. (And that's good news for the viewers, since we know the show has already been renewed for Season 3 .)

But first, a recap of the finale: Nadia's fatal car accident is the final straw for Callie, who reveals every single one of Margo's misdeeds to Sheriff Jonny. (Well, the ones she thinks she knows about, anyway.) Recognizing the love that Callie and Nadia shared, Jonny promises to get justice... but that promise is no match for Jed's offer to bring Jonny with him when he's elected Governor of Texas, so Jonny drops the issue, much to Callie's disapproval.

And Jonny isn't the only one who makes a deal with Jed. Margo, who initially intends to sink her husband's campaign and run away with Sophie, instead makes a different arrangement. She'll remain his dutiful wife as political career advances, and he'll once again make Callie and Sophie's legal troubles go away — as long they stay away from each other. But that's not good enough for Sophie, who also demands that Margo transfer $10 million into her bank account, or else she'll go public with Margo's recorded confession. "You cross this line, there's no coming back," Margo says, forgetting one thing: crossing the line is Sophie's favorite pastime.

The finale ends with Callie using a picture of Margo for target practice, Sophie anxiously waiting for the $10 million to land in her account, and Margo smiling alongside her husband on the campaign trail. Two years later, however, their stories are very different: an extremely well-dressed Sophie drops her black card at a swanky bar, where the news is reporting on Jed and Margo's latest push for anti-LGBTQ+ legislation. Sophie rightly acknowledges her ex-lover's hypocrisy, along with another choice word, before receiving a phone call from an unknown number. Surprise! It's Margo, breathing heavily... and covered in blood.

Netflix Even though we don't actually see the $10 million transfer into Sophie's account, showrunner Rebecca Perry Cutter confirms to TVLine that "the flash forward heavily implies that she got the money." As for who Margo may or may not have killed before calling Sophie, Cutter says the entire situation was a "really fun challenge."

entertainment.title: Morgan Freeman Voiced Frederick Douglass In A '90s Civil War Miniseries
entertainment.summary: Morgan Freeman lent his distinctive voice to Frederick Douglass in a landmark PBS miniseries, and the director had high praise for his performance.
entertainment.body:
Directed by historical documentarian Ken Burns, "The Civil War" explores the four-year American Civil War and its impact on the country. Burns told the Los Angeles Times in 1990 that Freeman's performance was "the best single voice in the film."

"[Freeman] speaks from this low volcanic voice and anger and he comes back up with truth that is undeniable," the director explained, adding that he'd tell him, "Be angry, be angrier, now be dignified."

"The Civil War" was a critical and ratings success , becoming PBS' most-watched series in a decade. It also helped popularize what became known as the Ken Burns effect, a filmmaking technique that emphasizes panning across or zooming in or out on still images.

Years later, Freeman co-executive produced the limited series "The Gray House" alongside Kevin Costner. The historical Prime Video series tells the story of four women who spied for the Union during the American Civil War.

The Oscar winner explained in February 2026 that he is drawn to historical projects because much of history remains untold, and he feels a responsibility to shine a light on those stories.

"There's a nail and I want to hit it right on the head," he said on "The View" while discussing "The Gray House." "This country, we don't know our history because so much of it is buried. ... The time has come for us to break that barrier."

Travis Barker is thankful for all the small things he shares with Rocky Barker .

Especially as the Blink-182 drummer revealed that he and wife Kourtney Kardashian ’s 3-year-old son share the exact same taste in Vans sneakers.

“We have a version of my black Dues Paid and a version of my white ones that are all studded out and he has ‘em too,” Barker shared in a recent interview with Complex . “And it’s his go-tos.”

entertainment.title: An Original South Park Star Had A Recurring Role On James Garner's The Rockford Files
entertainment.summary: Before starring as a fondly remembered character on "South Park," this actor played a memorable role in three episodes of "The Rockford Files" in the 1970s.
entertainment.body:
Comedy Central/YouTube Add TVLine on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover It's been 20 years since "South Park" killed off Chef (Isaac Hayes), and fans still miss him. Chef was a much-needed voice of wisdom for the unruly young main characters throughout the first seven seasons.

Unfortunately, Isaac Hayes suffered from a serious stroke in January 2006, and in March 2006 he released a statement criticizing the show's depiction of Scientology, quitting the show in protest. It wouldn't be until a decade later that Hayes' son revealed the actor had never actually written that statement; someone in the Church of Scientology had taken advantage of Hayes' incapacitated state to put words in his mouth. Hayes' departure from "South Park" may have been a mess , but even before that revelation, fans still remembered his character fondly.

The good news is that if you're a "South Park" fan who wants to hear Chef's voice again, you can get that on the '70s drama "The Rockford Files." James Garner was the main star of that show, but Hayes played a memorable guest star in three separate episodes. He played Gandolph Finch, AKA Gandy, and was introduced in the 1976 episode "The Hammer of C Block" as a former prisoner hoping to find his dead girlfriend's real killer. It was an incredibly dark episode, and it'd be the first of three massively critically acclaimed episodes of the series starring Hayes.

NBC/Roku In February 1977, Hayes' second episode on the show ("Just Another Polish Wedding") aired. In this one, Hayes plays a new version of Gandy, who was now a private eye. He and Rockford once again become an investigative duo, and their chemistry was off the charts.

Hayes' final "Rockford Files" outing was "Second Chance," and it aired in October 1977. In this one, Hayes plays a dive bar bouncer who's dating a singer with a haunted past named Theda, played by Dionne Warwick. The episode helped promote the new album "A Man and a Woman," a collaboration of Hayes' and Warwick's.

James Garner, who played the titular Rockford, praised the series for its "great characters" and included Hayes' Gandy among the best of them. "Isaac, his character, he was a big, tough, mean guy in prison, but I [Rockford] befriended him," he told the TV Academy Foundation . Garner himself passed away in 2014 , but "The Rockford Files" is being rebooted on NBC with David Boreanaz as the new lead. The new show is currently scheduled to premiere January 2, 2027, at 8 p.m. on NBC.

Hayes is perhaps best known for playing Julie Olson, the teen daughter of leads Addie Horton (Patricia Barry) and Ben Olson (Robert Knapp) and one of the original main characters when the show premiered in 1965. entertainment.title: Fuerza Regida Announces ‘Pisteando Con La Regida Vol. 4’ After Partial Legal Victory Against Rancho Humilde
entertainment.summary: “I’m free now they’ve finally taken their foot off the tiger’s neck,” frontman Jesús Ortiz Paz wrote in Spanish on Instagram.
entertainment.body:
Fuerza Regida is moving forward with new music following a partial legal victory in its ongoing dispute with regional Mexican label Rancho Humilde.

On Thursday (Nov. 26), the California-based música mexicana group, which graced Billboard ’s cover in October, announced that Pisteando Con La Regida Vol. 4 , the latest installment in its live album series, will arrive Dec. 3.

The project’s distribution partner has yet to be determined, with more details expected next week, a representative tells Billboard .

Fuerza Regida frontman Jesús Ortiz Paz revealed the album’s release date in an Instagram post featuring what appeared to be the project’s cover art. “I’m free now they’ve finally taken their foot off the tiger’s neck,” JOP wrote in Spanish alongside a photo gallery.

Fuerza Regida teased the project in October , when an Instagram post about 22 stolen live-performance videos included the hashtag #PisteandoConLaRegidaVol4, hinting at the title of the band’s upcoming album.

The PCLR Vol. 4 announcement comes one day after Fuerza Regida secured a legal victory against Rancho Humilde. On Wednesday (Nov. 25), a federal judge ruled that the label could no longer enforce its personal-services contract against the band’s four members beyond March 9, 2026, according to a ruling obtained by Billboard .

The dispute dates back to 2025, when Rancho Humilde sued the group over alleged breaches of its recording agreement. Fuerza Regida countersued , alleging the label had tried to “sabotage” its success. The group also claimed its deal with Rancho Humilde was void under California’s seven-year statute, which allows musicians to exit personal services contracts after that amount of time.

Judge Vera sided with Fuerza Regida on the seven-year statute question on Wednesday, though he noted in the decision that Rancho Humilde will be able to appeal. The rest of the lawsuit, including the claims for breach of contract, remains unresolved.

entertainment.body:
Joan Smalls is claiming that Candice Swanepoel got her “dropped” from a modeling gig amid tensions between the two over Swanepoel’s romance with Smalls’ ex, Tom Brady .

Three months after The Challenge winner died at the age of 44 , his cause of death was confirmed as heart disease.

According to TMZ , citing the North Dakota State Forensic Examiner’s Office, Tyler died of hypertensive cardiovascular disease, which is when the heart and blood vessels become damaged due to long-term high blood pressure. His death, per the outlet, was confirmed to be of natural causes.

Tyler’s mother Joni Duckworth shared the news of her son’s passing in an Aug. 13 Facebook post, noting she’d share service details “as soon as his dad and I figure it out.”

At the time, the Grand Forks Police Department told E! News that Tyler was found in a bathroom in his North Dakota apartment. Though they were still waiting on toxicology results at the time, police noted there were no signs of foul play, nor did Tyler’s death appear suspicious.

Before his success on The Challenge , which he won twice, Tyler made his reality TV debut on Real World: Key West in 2006. Following his passing, many of Tyler’s former reality TV costars from both shows paid him tribute, including Johnny “ Bananas ” Devenanzio .

“You were more than a friend," Johnny shared in a video posted to Instagram Aug. 15. "More than a roommate. You were the brother I never had. Rest easy, Tyler. You’ll always be family.”
